studies.title: Procurement managers admit they keep buying from suppliers they suspect of greenwashing
studies.paper_title: The greenwashing dilemma: Understanding tolerance to sustainability deception in buyer-supplier relationships
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with EU-based procurement managers, corporate sustainability managers and ESG consultants to understand "greenwashing tolerance" — the deliberate decision to keep doing business with a supplier whose sustainability claims look dubious. They found tolerance is propped up by relationship history and switching costs, which lower scrutiny and make confrontation expensive in the short run. Tolerance collapses mainly when a buyer concludes the deception was intentional and when the reputational exposure of being associated with it rises; only then does governance escalate from quiet remediation to sanctions and termination.
studies.why_it_matters: ESG claims in supply chains are increasingly treated as facts by regulators, investors and downstream customers, yet this suggests the buyers best positioned to police them often choose not to. It reframes greenwashing as a relational problem, not just a disclosure problem.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your firm's sustainability story depends on supplier disclosures, ask whether your own procurement team has the mandate, evidence and escalation path to challenge a long-standing supplier — the interviewees suggest layered verification and predefined escalation triggers are what convert suspicion into action. Worth auditing how many supplier ESG claims have ever been formally contested.
studies.story_angle_secondary: When a company tells you its supply chain is green, that assurance may rest on a claim someone internally privately doubts but finds too costly to challenge — a reminder that certification labels sit on top of commercial relationships people don't want to break.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample (19 interviews), EU only, self-reported accounts of sensitive behavior; the output is a conceptual framework and research propositions rather than measured effects on outcomes.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, sample (19 EU interviews), mechanisms and the conceptual-framework output are all reported faithfully; caveats match the abstract's own limitations.

studies.title: Micromanaging how salespeople spend their day makes the job feel meaningless — and performance suffers
studies.paper_title: Job meaningfulness in B2B salespeople: connecting salesforce control systems to B2B salesperson resilience and performance
studies.journal: The Journal of Marketing Theory and Practice
studies.the_study: A survey of 307 B2B salespeople, analyzed with structural equation modeling, tested how three styles of sales management control affect whether reps find their work meaningful. Outcome control (judging results) and capability control (developing skills) both raised perceived job meaningfulness, while activity control — dictating and monitoring day-to-day tasks — reduced it. Meaningfulness in turn predicted resilience, which was linked to higher job performance and lower intention to quit.
studies.why_it_matters: Sales organizations under pressure often respond by tightening activity tracking; this suggests that lever is the one most likely to drain motivation and increase churn in an already high-turnover role.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test whether your CRM activity quotas and call-logging mandates are buying you visibility at the cost of retention — and whether shifting the same managerial energy into coaching and capability-building produces better numbers. The correlational design means this is a hypothesis to run on your own salesforce data, not a settled result.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A concrete data point in the wider argument about workplace surveillance: being measured on outcomes or growth feels meaningful, while being measured on activity feels like being watched.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional self-report survey — cannot establish causation; performance and turnover intention are self-reported rather than observed; single sample with limited detail on country and industry mix.
studies.verdict_notes: N=307, SEM, the three control facets and the meaningfulness→resilience→performance/turnover chain all match; correlational limitation is flagged in both the body and caveats.

studies.title: Hard-closing salespeople damage buyer trust — and the buyers say so themselves
studies.paper_title: Differentiated selling behaviors and trust formation in industrial buyer–supplier relationships: a dyadic perspective
studies.journal: Journal of Business and Industrial Marketing
studies.the_study: Researchers collected matched survey data from 205 buyer–supplier pairs, asking the supplier side about salespeople's orientations and selling behaviors and the buyer side about trust and repurchase intention. Consultative selling raised both credibility-based and benevolence-based trust, while transactional, deal-pushing behavior was negatively associated with both. Credibility trust (belief in competence) predicted repurchase intention more strongly than benevolence trust (belief in goodwill).
studies.why_it_matters: Because the two sides of each relationship were surveyed separately, the finding is harder to dismiss as a salesperson's flattering self-assessment: the behaviors reps use to close faster appear to cost them the trust that drives renewal.
studies.story_angle_primary: Look at whether your incentive structure rewards transactional pushing in accounts you intend to keep for years, and consider that buyers weight demonstrated competence above perceived goodwill — advisory expertise and proof of capability may retain accounts better than relationship warmth.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Buyers can tell the difference between a salesperson solving their problem and one working a quota, and it changes whether they come back — a dynamic that plays out in consumer sales too.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey, so causal direction is unproven; regionally bounded sample; trust and repurchase intention are stated attitudes and intentions, not observed reorders.
studies.verdict_notes: Dyadic N=205 and all trust/repurchase findings are accurate; only the headline's causal verb overreaches a cross-sectional design.

studies.title: Keeping the same account team in place improves the customer experience — but discounts can undercut it
studies.paper_title: Customer experience–marketing alignment as a dynamic organisational capability: balancing structural continuity and behavioural adaptability
studies.the_study: A mixed-methods study of B2B customers in the UK used a two-wave, time-lagged survey (predictors and outcomes measured at different points) followed by interviews with a subset of respondents. Stability in the supplier's customer-facing team strengthened the effect of what the supplier offered on customers' factual, emotional and social experience, though not on their "sagacious" (insight-based) experience. Financial incentives had a split effect: they amplified the behavioral payoff of social experience but weakened the link between insight-based experience and buyer behavior.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests two common levers — account team continuity and discounting — pull in different directions, and that price incentives can crowd out the value customers place on a supplier's expertise.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before defending margin with discounts in strategic accounts, consider whether that spend is diluting the advisory value you've built; and treat account team stability as a deliberate investment rather than an HR accident. The time-lagged design strengthens the case, but this is one UK sample.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Continuity matters: dealing with the same people over time genuinely changes how good a service feels, which is part of why constant account-manager churn is so irritating.
studies.caveats: Single country (UK); sample size not reported in the abstract; survey-based measures of experience and behavior rather than transaction records; constructs such as "sagacious experience" are researcher-defined and may not map cleanly onto managerial categories.
studies.verdict_notes: Design and the split effect of financial incentives are reported correctly, but "financial incentives" is narrowed to "discounts" and the sagacious-experience result is softened.

studies.title: What Salespeople Say — and When They Say It — Decides Who Converts
studies.paper_title: EXPRESS: Ready to Convert? How to Talk with Sales Leads
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 783 recorded B2B lead-calling conversations comprising 11,566 individual speaking turns, coding salesperson speech into linguistic acts (legitimizing, piquing curiosity, nudging) and paralinguistic ones (volume intensity, speech rate, pitch), then modeling how each affected "lead receptivity" turn by turn and conversion at the call level. A one-standard-deviation rise in lead receptivity raised conversion likelihood by 13.44%. Timing mattered enormously: highly specific nudges lifted receptivity by 11.82% early in a call but cut it by 81.40% late in the call, and talking faster was neutral early but reduced receptivity by 8.26% later on.
studies.why_it_matters: It converts vague sales-call coaching into timing-specific rules drawn from real conversations, and shows the same tactic can help or backfire depending on where in the call it lands.
studies.story_angle_primary: Sales leaders can mine their own call recordings for these patterns and rebuild scripts and coaching around conversational phase rather than a fixed checklist — testing, for example, whether front-loading specific asks and slowing down in the back half of calls improves conversion in their own pipeline.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For anyone who has been on the receiving end of a cold call: the discomfort you feel when a rep pushes a concrete "so can we book Tuesday?" late in a conversation is measurable — and it is the single biggest documented killer of the sale.
studies.caveats: Observational data from a single lead-calling setting, so tactics are correlated with receptivity rather than randomized; the industry, product and language context of the calls limits how far the specific percentages generalize.
studies.verdict_notes: All figures (783 calls, 11,566 turns, 13.44%, 11.82%, 81.40%, 8.26%) reproduce the abstract exactly; the consumer angle overstates one illustrative effect.

studies.title: Three-Quarters of a Japanese Luxury Resale Chain's Revenue Came From Visitors, Not Locals
studies.paper_title: Value retention and non-resident demand in a Japanese second-hand luxury market: evidence from four years of multi-channel transaction records
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed a proprietary, complete four-year transaction record (348,745 records, 2018–2021) from a major Japanese second-hand luxury retailer, segmenting buyers by channel and residency into 12 personas and using a gradient-boosted model to characterize the corporate wholesale channel. Non-resident buyers accounted for 74% of consumer revenue (47.9–65.5% under stricter exclusions for likely procurement buying). When COVID-19 halted travel, the travel-dependent segment collapsed while domestic demand persisted; the wholesale-clearing channel recovered a median 54% of list price and was highly predictable (AUC 0.88).
studies.why_it_matters: It puts hard numbers on how dependent Asia-Pacific luxury resale is on cross-border shoppers, and gives retailers a quantified salvage value for unsold inventory plus a real-time demand indicator in the duty-free transaction share.
studies.story_angle_primary: Luxury and resale operators should test residency-by-channel segmentation on their own transaction data: concentrating authentication-heavy service on cross-border buyers, treating high-value repeat non-residents as key accounts, and pricing wholesale clearance against a known recovery rate rather than guesswork.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The booming "circular economy" story around second-hand luxury looks different up close — in this market, resale demand was powered largely by travelers and cross-border buyers, not by local shoppers trading up sustainably.
studies.caveats: Single retailer in a single country; buyers are identified by name-keying, and the split between genuine tourists and surrogate/daigou shoppers is bounded but not resolved; the period includes the unusual COVID travel shock.
studies.verdict_notes: Dataset size, 74% figure, robustness range, AUC 0.88 and 54% median recovery all match; the headline blurs "consumer revenue" and "non-resident buyers."

studies.title: Salespeople Proud of Their Employer Sell More — Unless They're Prouder of Their Profession
studies.paper_title: How retailer prestige drives sales performance and turnover: the mediating role of organizational identification and moderating role of professional identification
studies.the_study: A survey of 239 salespeople across 62 Brazilian retail stores selling building, electrical and painting materials tested how perceived retailer prestige — employees' beliefs about how outsiders rate their firm's status — translates into sales results. Prestige improved sales performance and reduced turnover intentions indirectly, through salespeople identifying with the organization. Counterintuitively, the link between organizational identification and sales performance was weaker among salespeople who strongly identified with their profession, though professional identification did not affect turnover intentions.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests employer-brand investment pays off on the sales floor mainly via a sense of belonging — and that the payoff is muted for staff whose primary loyalty is to their craft rather than the company.
studies.story_angle_primary: Retail and sales leaders can treat employer prestige as a performance lever, not just a recruiting one, while testing differentiated motivation: company-identity appeals for organization-oriented staff and craft, mastery and professional-development framing for those who see themselves as professionals first.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Why does a store's reputation shape the service you get? Staff who feel outsiders admire their employer behave differently — and workers who define themselves by their trade rather than their badge respond to entirely different motivations.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey in one country and one retail category, so causal direction cannot be established; self-reported measures including sales performance; results reflect stated intentions for turnover rather than observed departures.
studies.verdict_notes: N=239 across 62 Brazilian stores and the mediation/moderation structure are right; two small wording slips about the turnover result and direction of effects.

studies.title: An AI model beat seasoned B2B sales pros at calling which deals would close
studies.paper_title: Predicting sales offer success of industrial configure-to-order equipment: evaluating explainable AI approach with B2B sales experts
studies.the_study: Researchers worked with an industrial equipment maker that sells configure-to-order machinery, pulling real records from over 400 sales cases in the firm's CRM and Configure-Price-Quote systems. They trained a gradient-boosted decision tree (XGBoost) to predict win/loss outcomes and used SHAP values to explain each prediction, then pitted the model against experienced salespeople judging the same cases. The model hit 83.9% balanced accuracy on the full dataset and 74.1% on a regional subset, versus 63.0% and 54.4% for the human experts — the latter barely better than a coin flip. Five sales experts then reviewed the SHAP explanations and found them understandable and actionable, though some of the model's most predictive variables struck them as counterintuitive or unimportant.
studies.why_it_matters: Sales forecasting and opportunity prioritization still lean heavily on rep intuition, and this suggests that intuition can be substantially worse than a model trained on the firm's own CRM and quoting data.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before buying an AI sales-forecasting tool, run the cheaper test this paper models: score a few hundred historical closed deals with your own CRM data and benchmark the model against your reps' retrospective judgments. The explainability piece matters as much as the accuracy — the study's experts accepted the model partly because they could see which deal features drove each prediction, and the features they dismissed as irrelevant are exactly where a pipeline review might be leaving money on the table.
studies.story_angle_secondary: When a salesperson tells you they can 'read' a deal, this is a reminder that expert gut feel in complex commercial negotiations is often near-random — and that the patterns actually predicting outcomes may be ones no one in the room would guess.
studies.caveats: A single industrial firm in one product category (configure-to-order equipment), so results may not generalize; 400-plus cases is a modest dataset for machine learning, and the expert-evaluation component involved only five salespeople. The company was an industry partner in the research.
studies.verdict_notes: All accuracy figures, the 400+ cases, XGBoost/SHAP method and five-expert review match; the industry partner is disclosed in caveats. Only the consumer angle overgeneralizes.

studies.title: Meta-analysis: online product pages persuade along two separate tracks, and emotion doesn't work the way marketers assume
studies.paper_title: Click, Feel, Buy: How Online Presentations Shape Purchase Decision
studies.the_study: Researchers pooled two decades of fragmented studies on online product presentation — images, video, zoom, interactive and immersive displays — and combined them using meta-analysis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling. The synthesis found that cognitive responses and consumer involvement push purchase intention directly, while emotional responses only work indirectly, fully routed through attitude toward the product or brand. Effect sizes also varied systematically by region, gender, age and product type.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests product-page design has two distinct jobs — feeding deliberation and building affect — and that emotional appeal pays off only if it shifts how shoppers feel about the brand, not by prodding them straight to checkout.
studies.story_angle_primary: Treat the product page as a persuasion system with parallel paths rather than a single conversion lever: test information-rich elements (specs, comparisons, interactivity) against affect-building elements separately, and measure brand or product attitude as an intermediate metric rather than judging emotional creative purely on immediate conversion. The moderation results argue for localizing presentation formats by market, category and audience age rather than rolling out one global template.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The slick, emotive product video may not be what makes you click buy — evidence suggests it mostly changes how you feel about the item, and the click comes from the detail and hands-on interactivity that let you reason your way there.
studies.caveats: A synthesis of prior studies, so it inherits their reliance on stated purchase intention rather than observed purchases, and much of the underlying literature uses lab or online-panel designs. Meta-analytic structural models show associations across heterogeneous studies, not causal effects in any single retail setting; moderator breakdowns by region, gender and age depend on how the original studies were distributed.
studies.verdict_notes: The two-path finding, full mediation of emotion, and the four moderators are reported correctly; small additions of detail not present in the abstract.

studies.title: When suppliers play manipulative games, tighter contracts make distributors behave worse, not better
studies.paper_title: Manufacturer Machiavellianism and distributor opportunism in China
studies.the_study: A survey of 327 distributors in China measured how manipulative, Machiavellian behavior by manufacturers related to the distributors' own opportunistic conduct, using hierarchical regression to test moderators. Perceived manufacturer manipulation was strongly associated with more distributor opportunism. Crucially, deeply embedded relationships dampened the effect, whereas more complete, detailed contracts amplified it — as did market uncertainty and intense competition.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the reflex response to a fraying channel relationship, which is to write a tighter contract: if the partner already reads you as manipulative, more formal control may read as more evidence of bad faith.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit whether your channel-governance escalation path is actually making things worse — the study implies that contract tightening works only when trust is intact, and that relationship investment is the better lever once a partner suspects manipulation. Watch especially for markets in turbulence or under heavy competitive pressure, where the study found the manipulation-to-opportunism link strongest.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The finding echoes something familiar outside business: when people sense they're being handled, adding rules and fine print tends to fuel resistance rather than compliance.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey, so causal direction cannot be established — opportunistic distributors may also perceive their suppliers as more manipulative. All measures are distributor perceptions of their own and their partner's conduct, self-reported and vulnerable to bias, and the sample covers distributors in a single country (China).
studies.verdict_notes: N=327, method and all four moderators match the abstract; one managerial inference goes past what was tested.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies in this batch independently show that the standard corporate reflex — tighten control when a commercial relationship is under strain — makes outcomes worse. Micromanaging reps' daily activity drains job meaningfulness and raises quit intentions while outcome and capability coaching do the opposite ("Micromanaging how salespeople spend their day makes the job feel meaningless," W7211996947); writing more complete, detailed contracts amplifies rather than curbs distributor opportunism once a partner reads the supplier as manipulative ("When suppliers play manipulative games, tighter contracts make distributors behave worse," W7208824278); transactional deal-pushing measurably erodes buyer trust in matched buyer–supplier pairs ("Hard-closing salespeople damage buyer trust," W7172448511); and highly specific nudges that lift receptivity early in a call cut it by 81.40% when deployed late ("What Salespeople Say — and When They Say It — Decides Who Converts," W7203901346). Alongside them, "Procurement managers admit they keep buying from suppliers they suspect of greenwashing" (W7213538226) shows the mirror image: formal verification machinery that nobody is willing to trigger because the relationship costs too much.

**Why pitch this now:** Sales and procurement organizations are being handed more monitoring capability than ever — call recording, CRM activity dashboards, AI conversation scoring, ESG supplier-audit platforms — at exactly the moment revenue pressure makes leaders want to squeeze harder, and this evidence says the squeeze is where the leakage starts.

**Angle:** A reported feature for a management or CMO audience on the limits of control in commercial relationships: when does a contract clause, an activity quota, or a closing push stop buying compliance and start buying resentment — and what the alternative levers (coaching, account-team continuity, relational investment, evidence-based escalation triggers) actually look like in practice.

**Potential headlines:**
- Four new studies find that tightening control over sellers, buyers and channel partners backfires
- The contract clause that makes your distributor cheat you
- What your sales dashboard is quietly costing you in trust and turnover

**Potential outlets:**
- *Harvard Business Review* — the control-versus-trust tension in contracts and sales management is squarely its governance-and-leadership territory, and the channel study gives it a counterintuitive core finding to build on.
- *MIT Sloan Management Review* — strong fit for a piece weighing formal control mechanisms against relational governance, with the procurement/greenwashing material adding a supply-chain dimension.
- *Marketing Week* — B2B sales effectiveness and the incentive structures behind it are recurring beats, and the buyer–supplier trust data speaks directly to its commercial-effectiveness readership.
- *Fast Company* — the activity-monitoring findings slot into its ongoing coverage of workplace measurement and surveillance, with a fresh angle: the monitoring is hurting the numbers it was installed to protect.
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Procurement managers admit they keep buying from suppliers they suspect of greenwashing (Work ID W7213538226):** The people best placed to police ESG claims often choose not to because the relationship is too valuable to break — pitch as a sustainability-accountability story for a business or ESG trade section, with a sidebar on what escalation triggers would actually look like.
- **Micromanaging how salespeople spend their day makes the job feel meaningless (Work ID W7211996947):** Activity quotas and call-logging mandates buy visibility and cost retention, while coaching does the reverse — a CMO- or sales-leader column, or a workplace-surveillance item for a general-interest work section.
- **Hard-closing salespeople damage buyer trust — and the buyers say so themselves (Work ID W7172448511):** Matched buyer and supplier surveys make this hard to dismiss as rep self-flattery, and competence trust beats warmth for driving repurchase — a marketing-trade news brief or a sales-incentive-design column.
- **Keeping the same account team in place improves the customer experience — but discounts can undercut it (Work ID W7171153525):** Account-team continuity is an unmanaged asset, and discounting can crowd out the advisory value a supplier has built — a B2B marketing trade explainer or a key-account-management feature.
- **What Salespeople Say — and When They Say It — Decides Who Converts (Work ID W7203901346):** Nearly 12,000 coded speaking turns turn vague call coaching into phase-specific rules, including an 81.40% receptivity drop for late-call specific nudges — a strong marketing-trade news piece, and a consumer-psychology explainer on why cold calls feel the way they do.
- **Three-Quarters of a Japanese Luxury Resale Chain's Revenue Came From Visitors, Not Locals (Work ID W7204571119):** The circular-economy narrative around second-hand luxury looks very different when the demand turns out to be travel-driven — a retail trade explainer, or a consumer-economics piece on tourism, daigou buying and resale pricing.
- **Salespeople Proud of Their Employer Sell More — Unless They're Prouder of Their Profession (Work ID W7202160517):** Employer brand as a sales-performance lever rather than a recruitment one, with a twist for craft-identified staff — an HR/employer-brand trade column or a retail-management piece.
- **An AI model beat seasoned B2B sales pros at calling which deals would close (Work ID W7204437044):** Experts scored barely above a coin flip on a regional subset while an explainable model hit 83.9% balanced accuracy — pitch as a sales-tech news story, plus a practical "run this test before you buy the tool" column for a CMO or revenue-operations audience.
- **Meta-analysis: online product pages persuade along two separate tracks (Work ID W7204660594):** Emotional creative works only by shifting brand attitude, never straight to checkout — an e-commerce or performance-marketing trade explainer arguing for brand attitude as an intermediate metric.
- **When suppliers play manipulative games, tighter contracts make distributors behave worse (Work ID W7208824278):** Contract tightening only works while trust is intact; once a partner reads you as manipulative, fine print reads as proof — a channel-management or supply-chain trade piece, and a management column on the limits of formal control.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — B2B & Sales — 2026-09-21
**Checked:** 2026-09-21 | **Studies reviewed:** 10
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: Procurement managers admit they keep buying from suppliers they suspect of greenwashing
**Work ID:** W7213538226 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 2: Micromanaging how salespeople spend their day makes the job feel meaningless — and performance suffers
**Work ID:** W7211996947 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 3: Hard-closing salespeople damage buyer trust — and the buyers say so themselves
**Work ID:** W7172448511 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal headline for cross-sectional survey** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Hard-closing salespeople damage buyer trust — and the buyers say so themselves"
- **Abstract says:** "transactional selling behaviour is negatively associated with both trust dimensions … The cross-sectional and regionally bounded sample limits generalizability."
- **Problem:** "Damage" asserts causation from a cross-sectional matched survey; the abstract states only a negative association, and the digest's own caveat concedes causal direction is unproven.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to something like "Hard-closing salespeople are linked to lower buyer trust — and the buyers say so themselves.""

### Study 4: Keeping the same account team in place improves the customer experience — but discounts can undercut it
**Work ID:** W7171153525 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Financial incentives" recast as "discounts"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Before defending margin with discounts in strategic accounts, consider whether that spend is diluting the advisory value you've built"
- **Abstract says:** "the use of financial incentives jointly shape CX and subsequent buyer behaviour … Financial incentives weaken the link between sagacious experience and behaviour but enhance the effect of social experience."
- **Problem:** The abstract measures financial incentives generally (which could include rebates, bonuses or volume terms), not discounting specifically; the headline and angle both substitute "discounts."
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "financial incentives" and note that the abstract does not specify which incentive types were studied."

**Issue B. Sagacious-experience effect understated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "though not on their "sagacious" (insight-based) experience"
- **Abstract says:** "while limiting the impact on sagacious experience"
- **Problem:** "Limiting the impact" implies team stability dampened the offering–sagacious experience link, which is a different result from simply having no effect.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "while limiting the effect on their 'sagacious' (insight-based) experience.""

**Issue C. Moderation described as a main effect** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Keeping the same account team in place improves the customer experience"
- **Abstract says:** "the stability of the supplier's interacting team strengthens the influence of supplier offerings on CX"
- **Problem:** Team stability is reported as a moderator that strengthens the offering–CX link, not as a direct driver of customer experience.
- **Suggested fix:** "Headline could read "Keeping the same account team in place amplifies what a supplier's offering does for customer experience.""

### Study 5: What Salespeople Say — and When They Say It — Decides Who Converts
**Work ID:** W7203901346 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Superlative claim not in the abstract** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the discomfort you feel when a rep pushes a concrete "so can we book Tuesday?" late in a conversation is measurable — and it is the single biggest documented killer of the sale"
- **Abstract says:** "For instance, more specific (compared to less specific) nudges increase lead receptivity by 11.82% earlier in the conversation but reduce it by 81.40% later in the conversation."
- **Problem:** The abstract presents the late-nudge effect as one illustrative example of a turn-level effect on lead receptivity, not on sales outcomes, and makes no claim that it is the largest documented factor in lost sales.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop "single biggest documented killer of the sale" and say the late specific nudge was associated with a sharp drop in the lead's receptivity in that turn."

**Issue B. Paralinguistic label expanded** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "paralinguistic ones (volume intensity, speech rate, pitch)"
- **Abstract says:** "paralinguistic acts (intensity, speech rate, pitch)"
- **Problem:** The abstract says "intensity" without specifying volume; the interpretation is plausible but not stated.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "intensity, speech rate, pitch" as in the abstract."

### Study 6: Three-Quarters of a Japanese Luxury Resale Chain's Revenue Came From Visitors, Not Locals
**Work ID:** W7204571119 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline scope of the 74% figure** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Three-Quarters of a Japanese Luxury Resale Chain's Revenue Came From Visitors, Not Locals"
- **Abstract says:** "Non-resident buyers carry 74% of consumer revenue (47.9–65.5% under stricter procurement exclusions)."
- **Problem:** The 74% applies to consumer revenue only (the study separately analyzes a corporate wholesale channel), and "visitors" implies tourists when the abstract states the tourist-versus-daigou composition is bounded, not resolved.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "three-quarters of consumer revenue came from non-resident buyers" and keep the tourist/daigou ambiguity visible in the headline or standfirst."

### Study 7: Salespeople Proud of Their Employer Sell More — Unless They're Prouder of Their Profession
**Work ID:** W7202160517 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Moderation result restated as a main effect** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "though professional identification did not affect turnover intentions"
- **Abstract says:** "However, this moderating effect does not extend to turnover intentions."
- **Problem:** The abstract says professional identification did not moderate the identification–turnover link; it makes no claim about whether professional identification affects turnover intentions at all.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write "though professional identification did not moderate the link to turnover intentions.""

**Issue B. Direction of the turnover effect assumed** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Prestige improved sales performance and reduced turnover intentions indirectly, through salespeople identifying with the organization."
- **Abstract says:** "retailer organizational prestige indirectly affects sales performance and turnover intentions through organizational identification"
- **Problem:** The abstract states an indirect effect without specifying the direction for turnover intentions; "reduced" (and "improved") is an inference and also reads causally for a cross-sectional survey.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "was indirectly associated with sales performance and turnover intentions" unless the direction can be confirmed from the full text."

### Study 8: An AI model beat seasoned B2B sales pros at calling which deals would close
**Work ID:** W7204437044 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Generalizing one firm's expert panel to expert judgment at large** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "expert gut feel in complex commercial negotiations is often near-random"
- **Abstract says:** "The model achieved balanced accuracies of 83.9% on the full dataset and 74.1% on a regional subset, substantially outperforming expert predictions, which reached 63.0 and 54.4%, respectively."
- **Problem:** The 54.4% figure comes from one regional subset at a single industrial partner; extending it to expert intuition "in complex commercial negotiations" generally goes beyond the evidence and sits awkwardly with the digest's own generalizability caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "Limit the claim to this setting, e.g. "in this firm's regional cases, expert judgment was little better than chance.""

### Study 9: Meta-analysis: online product pages persuade along two separate tracks, and emotion doesn't work the way marketers assume
**Work ID:** W7204660594 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Mediator specified beyond the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "emotional responses only work indirectly, fully routed through attitude toward the product or brand"
- **Abstract says:** "the effect of emotion is fully mediated by consumer attitude"
- **Problem:** The abstract says "consumer attitude" without specifying product or brand attitude; the digest adds that distinction and then builds a measurement recommendation on it.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "fully routed through consumer attitude" and drop the product/brand specification."

**Issue B. Presentation formats listed but not named in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "fragmented studies on online product presentation — images, video, zoom, interactive and immersive displays"
- **Abstract says:** "Online product presentation is the e-commerce equivalent of the salesperson … in an increasingly immersive, technology driven retail environment."
- **Problem:** The specific formats included in the meta-analysis are not listed in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Either drop the list or attribute it as an example of the formats such research typically covers."

### Study 10: When suppliers play manipulative games, tighter contracts make distributors behave worse, not better
**Work ID:** W7208824278 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Untested inference about when contracts help** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the study implies that contract tightening works only when trust is intact, and that relationship investment is the better lever once a partner suspects manipulation"
- **Abstract says:** "contract completeness, market uncertainty and industry competitive intensity strengthen the positive relationship between manufacturer Machiavellianism and distributor opportunism … Relationship embeddedness mitigates this effect."
- **Problem:** The study tested contract completeness as a moderator of the Machiavellianism–opportunism link; it did not test whether contracts work when trust is intact, nor did it compare relational investment against contracting as interventions.
- **Suggested fix:** "Limit the angle to what was found: more complete contracts were associated with more, not less, opportunism where manipulation was perceived, while embedded relationships buffered it."
